item.title: The resurrection of Jensen Huang. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As news of the polyamorous relationships of Jensen Huang, the Taiwan-born CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies , NVIDIA, hit headlines worldwide, Nvidia announced his resignation on November 12.
On November 23, the board unanimously reinstated him. Jensen Huang’s resurrection was as spectacular as his fall.
Powerful beings can resurrect fallen ones. It is evident now that the President Donald Trump had to influence the corporate board of NVIDIA to rehire Jensen Huang. Recently, The Economist in early September 2026 ran a major story on NVIDIA featuring Huang on its cover under the title "The Sorcerer of Silicon." That headline proved remarkably prescient. Little did the venerable publication know that in the ensuing days, Huang would suffer a dramatic fall from grace and require a magic wand to regain his throne.
Yet the true magic wand was not President Donald Trump himself, but the sharp plunge of NVIDIA’s stock price, which sent tremors through Wall Street. The modern corporate world has become the new site of wizardry, and its opacity rivals that of ancient sorcery.
Behind closed doors, algorithms, valuations, and executive allegiances operate like arcane rituals largely invisible to the public eye. When the spell broke and NVIDIA’s shares tumbled, the illusion of pure market autonomy evaporated just as quickly.
As shareholders -- including, presumably, Trump and his political allies -- watched immense wealth vanish while NVIDIA’s valuation plummeted, the White House stepped in. Trump intervened not so much out of personal loyalty to save his friend, but to save Wall Street from a systemic spiral.
In an economy increasingly tethered to the fortunes of a handful of artificial intelligence giants, the fate of one chief executive became indistinguishable from the stability of the broader financial market. When a single company’s market capitalization carries the weight of national economic confidence, corporate governance ceases to be a private affair.
Ironically, even many vocal critics of the US p resident found themselves quietly relieved by the outcome. On the surface, the episode reads like a classic tale of high politics watching the back of high finance -- an unvarnished display of crony capitalism in which state power bends corporate accountability to protect the powerful.
Progressive commentators and institutional purists alike routinely decry executive overreach into private enterprise. Yet when retirement portfolios, index funds, and market stability hang in the balance, ideological objections soften into pragmatic silence. Wall Street’s sigh of relief was bipartisan, even if whispered behind closed doors.
Beyond the immediate drama of stock tickers and presidential phone calls, the Jensen Huang affair is rich in moral and sociological insights.
More than a century ago, the French master sociologist Émile Durkheim reminded us that it is precisely by deviating from moral rules that a society becomes conscious of what those rules actually are. In Durkheim’s view, a breach of conventions is not merely a failure of order; it serves a vital social function. By testing the boundaries of acceptable behaviour, a scandal forces the collective conscience to confront its own unspoken values, hypocrisies, and limits.
Huang’s ouster and rapid reinstatement expose the deeply conflicted moral code of contemporary capitalism. On one hand, corporate governance preaches strict accountability, fiduciary duty, and the principle that no leader -- no matter how visionary -- is above the rules of the boardroom.
On the other hand, modern financial markets worship indispensable founders, treating technological visionaries as irreplaceable demi-gods whose removal threatens economic ruin.
When those two principles collided, accountability wa s lost. The board’s initial decision to remove Huang affirmed the formal rules of corporate oversight; his swift resurrection revealed the informal rule that actually governs our age: T oo big to fail now applies not just to banks, but to individual CEOs.
At the same time, the episode lays bare the fiction of the self-regulating free market. For decades, orthodox economic wisdom insisted that the government should stay out of corporate boardrooms and allow market forces to reward or punish executives without political interference.
Yet when the market delivered a verdict that threatened broader financial pain, the highest political office in the land was summoned to reverse it.
State intervention, long demonized when deployed to protect workers or consumers, was suddenly embraced as indispensable when deployed to steady equity prices.
Durkheim argued that when a society reacts to a violation of its norms, it clarifies what it truly holds sacred. Looking at the resurrection of Jensen Huang, the answer is unmistakable.
What modern capitalism holds sacred is neither free-market purity nor boardroom integrity, but uninterrupted market momentum. The rules of governance, the boundaries between the state and the corporation, and the rhetoric of accountability all remain intact -- until the stock chart turns sharply downward.
In the end, Jensen Huang has returned to his post, the markets have caught their breath, and the sorcery of Silicon Valley resumes its familiar hum.
But the spell of corporate independence has been broken, revealing the curtain, and what we found there was not an invisible hand, but a very visible presidential one -- reminding us that in the high-stakes theatre of global finance, resurrection is always possible, provided the price of falling is too high for the powerful to bear.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: A physician's diagnosis of Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Sheikh Hasina says she will come home in December, despite what she calls "the threat of death." The law minister says the legal process for her return is complete, and that the decision now rests with New Delhi.
Within those two sentences lies the whole condition of Bangladesh: A question that belongs to Bangladeshis, waiting on the answer of another capital.
In the past fortnight, the mere prospect of her return has drawn blood. In Faridpur, a bus driver died after his bus was set on fire. In Gopalganj, her home district, a police station was stormed and burned. Police say two members of the ruling party have been killed, and the ancestral home of Muhammad Yunus has been set ablaze.
That is the fever. A physician who treats only the fever loses the patient. What follows is about the illness beneath it.
I am not a politician. I am a physician, writing from Stockholm. When I was 15, my father wanted me to study international relations; life sent me to medical school instead. But I have carried Bangladesh inside me since the early 1970s: The communal tensions, the quarrel with India, the quiet thinning of the Hindu population.
In August I asked in these pages that Bangladesh not be bullied, by anyone. Medicine has taught me one thing that politics often forgets. Shouting does not cure a patient. First comes a diagnosis, then a treatment.
The history
Every sound diagnosis begins with the history, and the history of Bangladesh begins before 1971. It begins in 1947, when the subcontinent was cut along the line of faith. That wound never fully closed.
Liberation in 1971 was meant to be the answer: A nation founded on language and land, not on the book one prays from. Within four years, after the bloodshed of 1975, that answer was already being revised. Ever since, the old sore of 1947 has been reopened, sometimes by politicians, sometimes by fear.
Today's troubles sit on top of it like a fresh injury on an old scar. A doctor who treats only the fresh injury will be surprised, again and again, when the patient does not heal.
The diagnosis
I see two conditions, and they feed each other.
The first is the identity crisis. Bengali or Muslim? The colour of the passport, or the colour of the holy book? I have argued in these pages that this is a pseudo-crisis: One can be wholly Bengali and wholly Muslim, or Hindu, or Christian, as generations of our grandparents were without asking anyone's permission. But a false illness can still make a patient very sick if the patient believes in it. It drains the household's energy, sets brother against brother, and leaves the weakest members of the family, the minorities, most exposed.
Consider a thought experiment for readers far from Dhaka. In 1951, more than one in five people in what is now Bangladesh was Hindu. Today it is fewer than one in 12, and in 2016 the Dhaka University economist Abul Barkat warned that, at the pace of the past half-century, none would remain within 30 years.
Picture the same arc in the United States: Catholics shrinking within one lifetime from a fifth of the nation to an anxious remnant, American Jews close to vanishing. No one would call that a minority issue. They would call it the unmaking of America, because an America without its Catholics and its Jews would not be the same country with fewer people. It would be a different country.
So it is with Bangladesh. The Bengali identity that won 1971 was woven from Hindu and Muslim threads alike: Tagore and Nazrul, puja and Eid. Pull one thread out entirely and the cloth does not merely shrink. It unravels.
The second condition is geography. India surrounds Bangladesh on three sides; the Bay of Bengal is the fourth. India, like every state, pursues its own interests, and those interests are chiefly security and trade. It is what states do, and Washington, Beijing, and Moscow do the same. The difficulty is not that India has interests. It is that Bangladesh has too often failed to state its own with equal clarity, swinging instead between dependence and resentment.
Now see how the two conditions interact. When identity is unsettled at home, every relationship abroad becomes a referendum on who we are. Friendship with India is called betrayal; hostility to India is called patriotism; and the Hindus of Bangladesh are made to answer for a neighbour's policies. A nation unsure of itself cannot negotiate firmly with anyone.
The treatment
Chronic conditions are rarely cured; they are managed. Geography is chronic. You cannot wish away a neighbour. You can only choose the terms on which you live beside it. The identity crisis, being false, can be resolved. Neither treatment can be imported. Both must be prescribed at home.
This is where Sheikh Hasina's case belongs. I offer no verdict here. Bangladeshis hold strong and painful views, and a tribunal in Dhaka has sentenced her to death for the crackdown of 2024. My point is narrower, and I hope it is one that all sides can share.
Whatever Bangladesh decides about her, it must be Bangladesh that decides, through its own courts, under its own law, with a due process the world can respect. Not New Delhi, not Washington, not Beijing, not Moscow. A nation that cannot settle its own past in its own house has not yet finished becoming a nation.
The prognosis
In January, my nephew, an American raised in a Bengali Hindu family, will bring his Canadian bride, a Catholic Christian, to Bangladesh. They have already married in a church. Now they want a Bengali wedding, with the turmeric of the gaye holud and the whole noisy, loving family around them. An American, a Canadian Catholic, and a Hindu family will gather in a Muslim-majority country to celebrate a Bengali marriage.
If Bangladesh can host that without fear, the prognosis is not hopeless. The patient has a strong constitution. Since 1971 it has survived storms from every direction. But survival is not the same as strength.
What Bangladesh still lacks is a spine, and a spine is built from within: an identity at peace with itself, and the confidence to deal with every neighbour, large or small, on its own terms.
That treatment is in Bangladesh's own hands. No other capital can prescribe it.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

item.title: RMG wage crisis: Who pays for growth, and who pays the price?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The readymade garments’ (RMG) industry in Bangladesh is once again confronting a serious labour crisis. Workers were protesting on the streets in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia, Narayanganj, and Dhaka for the minimum wage of Tk 30,000 per month, which is currently Tk 12,500. In early November, when unrest was at its peak, the BGMEA said that 529 factories had suspended production, putting nearly a million workers out of work.
The government acted swiftly. The six-member wage board was established on November 1 and both sides have agreed to the effectivity of the new wage board from December 1 with a revised wage to take effect in January.
Workers have a case The minimum wage was last hiked in late 2023 from Tk 8,000 to Tk 12,500. Much of this increase has since been lost amid three years of high inflation. The inflation rate was 8.27% in October 2026. Food prices have slowed, but non-food inflation is increasing to 9.89% , its highest level in 41 months, and a worker's budget is being dominated by rent, transport, healthcare, and schooling costs. According to official data, inflation is now running at a higher rate than wages for 57 months in a row. The Clean Clothes Campaign (CCC) (in May and August, 2026) survey of 1,094 garment workers, carried out from May to August, revealed that 89% were unable to pay their basic expenses for their families; 70% of the workers took loans from friends or relatives, and 28% took the loans from additional overtime. These early results are in line with what reporters are hearing on the ground. Workers are being forced to take difficult decisions like meals eliminated, medical care deferred, and children removed from school.
However, the jobs argument is a two-way paradigm. The cost of labour is about 10-13% of industry costs. International experience, as in Germany with a minimum wage, indicates that job loss is not inevitable, but instead varies with the extent and speed of the wage increase and the capacity of firms to respond. Unrest also leads to factory closures, cancelled shipments, and job losses, and buyers are aware that a marginally cheaper supplier is an expensive supplier if their production is continually disrupted.
The missing party at the table
The global buyer is the most under-heard player in this debate. Brands are driving ever higher standards for safety, environment, traceability, and carbon reporting, and are tough to bargain with regarding price.
A previous ILO survey revealed that there is little evidence that buyers were willing to pass on minimum wage increases to Bangladeshi suppliers. A wage increase that the buyer will not partake in is pushed back onto the factories and, ultimately, onto the owners and workers.
Responsible sourcing and practices that squeeze suppliers cannot coexist. When brands promote decent work, they should make this commitment publicly and in their contracts to pay for the labour-cost share of the new wage, whether through ring-fenced wage components in the order prices, or with longer term sourcing commitments. There should be a coordinated push by the BGMEA, BKMEA, and the government, not only by the factories.
A national problem
The RMG sector currently supports about four million jobs, the majority of which are held by women, and generates over 80% of the income from merchandise exports. The delay of shipments in the peak season also affects factory cash flows and foreign-exchange receipts; it also reduces the spending of workers’ households.
The unrest has also caused anxiety among buyers as Bangladesh is preparing for its graduation from the LDC category and the end of trade preferences. The economy can ill afford another self-inflicted blow as private-sector credit growth is around 4%.
There are four steps that would help to break the cycle.
First of all , the wage board’s decision must be based upon transparent evidence: Household expenditure, inflation, productivity, and industry capacity. They must also state their reasoning for the decision. The schedule must be short, front-loaded, binding, and not be postponed.
Secondly , the new labour law stipulates that annual changes should only occur between full revisions in every three years; this should be adjusted to inflation.
Third , small factories should be put on alert. Identify sources of working capital, a stable supply of energy, a stable source of productivity training, and a commitment to full implementation of the new wage.
Fourth , industrial relations need to be formalized in the institutional structure of independent trade unions, working participation committees, and effective grievance procedures, and blacklisting and retaliation against workers who protest must stop.
The choice Bangladesh cannot postpone
Bangladesh is the second biggest apparel exporter in the world. Yet, much of this has been due to its low labour cost - an advantage that is fading and one that’s never been a strong base. Its future competitiveness must be based on productivity, skills, technology, and higher value products, rather than retaining low-paid employees.
A garment industry that exports prosperity to the world but cannot adequately sustain the livelihoods of its own workers is not a model of sustainable development. Bangladesh must now decide whether it wants to remain a low-wage manufacturing destination or become a globally competitive economy built on productive, skilled and fairly compensated workers.
Dr Md Sohel Rana is an Associate Professor, IUBAT Business School.

item.title: What the ICJ’s landmark genocide finding could mean for the case against Israel in Gaza. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) last week ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority group.
The court found Myanmar breached its obligations under the United Nations genocide convention to prevent and punish genocide.
This ruling is not just important for the Rohingya and Myanmar. It may also have a significant legal impact on other genocide cases before the court -- in particular, South Africa’s case alleging Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.
Other genocide cases
Four cases currently before the ICJ concern allegations of breaches of the genocide convention.
One was brought by Ukraine against Russia following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Another was brought by Nicaragua against Germany, regarding Germany’s support of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The third was brought by the Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwanda, which includes claims about Rwanda’s involvement in conflict in the Kivu provinces of the DRC.
The Myanmar ruling may have repercussions for all these cases.
However, the judgement will mostly affect the fourth genocide case before the court, the one brought by South Africa against Israel.
Multiple intents
Genocide is different from “ordinary” crimes in that it requires a “special intent” (or dolus specialis) -- the intent to destroy a national, racial, ethnic or religious group, in whole or in part.
This must be proven in addition to a general criminal intent, where a perpetrator intends to commit the crime or could have foreseen the result of their actions.
Genocidal intent is proven by two main forms of evidence. Firstly, there are the statements of political and military leaders, soldiers, the media and key figures in society. These often dehumanise the targeted group and may explicitly refer to the destruction of the group in some way.
The second way intent is proven is by looking at the perpetrators’ pattern of conduct.
In the Myanmar case, the court considered hate speech by Myanmar authorities against the Rohingya to be incitement to genocide. This formed evidence of intent.
The judges also used the military’s pattern of conduct to determine intent. Myanmar argued its intent was a counterinsurgency operation against a terrorist group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA). But the court determined the conduct of Myanmar’s security forces did not align with an intent to carry out a genuine counterinsurgency operation.
The court held that acts such killing civilians (including children), raping women, and destroying villages did not form part of legitimate military operations -- even if the operation also had the intent of meeting military objectives.
This is significant for the Israel genocide case because Israel argues it is fighting in self-defense in Gaza against a terrorist group, Hamas.
However, statements from Israeli government ministers about the intention to deny Palestinians necessities of life, or to erase Palestine from the map, may suggest a different intent.
As in the Myanmar case, the violence in Gaza has included the killing of civilians (including children), the widespread destruction of buildings (including in residential areas), and sexual and gender-based violence.
The Myanmar judgement gives the court an opening to decide that Israel has had both an intent to fight Hamas and a genocidal intent. Or it could decide Israel’s operations in Gaza do not represent a legitimate and lawful way to carry out an anti-terrorism military operation, which may demonstrate clear genocidal intent.
Killing of children
One of the key aspects of The Gambia’s case against Myanmar was that the killing of children demonstrated genocidal intent. The reason: Killing children is not a legitimate military objective.
The ICJ agreed. The court held that the killing of up to 2,000 children under the age of five was a significant indicator that Myanmar intended to destroy the future of the Rohingya people.
According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, Israel has killed almost 22,000 children under 18 in Gaza. Some have been killed in indiscriminate attacks. Others have been deliberately targeted, according to the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.
Following the court’s Myanmar decision, the killing of so many children in Gaza may strengthen the case against a legitimate military operation, and that the military and therefore the state instead had genocidal intent.
Broader context of crimes
The Myanmar case focused on the so-called “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in 2017. However, this violence was placed in the context of a lengthy history of discrimination and persecution of the Rohingya.
The court recognized that violations of human rights, which may not necessarily amount to genocidal crimes, were part of the bigger picture of the genocide. The exclusion of the Rohingya from citizenship was one example, as it denied them access to education, employment, healthcare, food and free movement.
Similarly, South Africa’s case against Israel positions the violence in Gaza since 2023 as an escalating step in decades of discrimination and persecution -- a system of apartheid -- against Palestinians.
Scale and targeting of crimes
ICJ judges also recognized that the scale of the crimes in Myanmar was relevant to the finding that genocide occurred, alongside the fact the violence specifically targeted the Rohingya. Thousands of Rohingya were killed and raped, and myriad Rohingya villages were destroyed. Non-Rohingya were not attacked, and their villages were not burned.
This has parallels to the situation in Gaza. Large numbers of Palestinians have been killed and injured, and huge swathes of Gaza have been destroyed.
It is estimated it will take many years and billions of dollars to clear and rebuild Gaza.
These findings have clear parallels with the situation in Gaza, and will undoubtedly be drawn on by South Africa as its case against Israel progresses in the coming years.
Melanie O'Brien is Professor of International Law, The University of Western Australia. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

item.title: Making plastic rules practical. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Adopting a European-style extended producer responsibility (EPR) framework to tackle plastic pollution is a welcome shift in policy ambition, moving the nation toward binding accountability for manufacturers, importers, and brand owners.
It was clear that merely relying primarily on government agencies and informal waste collectors was not sustainable nor fair. To that end, holding businesses accountable for the plastic they put on the market is the right way.
It goes without saying that plastic pollution continues to devastate our country. The result is choking canals, waterlogged streets, microplastics in food chains, and clogged drainage networks - all of which make aggressive action against plastic waste non-negotiable.
With that said, we agree with the concerns voiced by experts that importing a European regulatory model onto a very different economic landscape could fail unless the measures are grounded in feasibility, clear enforcement, and realistic local capacity.
The real test, as with any new policy or initiative, lies in practical execution rather than announcements. Shifting waste costs onto producers only reduces pollution if collection targets are verifiable, local sorting hubs exist, and companies cannot game the system through paper credits or unverified claims.
At the same time, slapping abrupt, uncalibrated compliance burdens onto smaller businesses or overlooking informal pickers and recyclers risks either driving activity underground or hurting livelihoods without cutting waste.
To make this framework work, the government must assist with practical infrastructure: Standardizing recyclable packaging, supporting local material recovery and recycling capacity, coordinating municipal waste collection, and integrating informal collectors into formal supply chains with fair protections are all steps that must be considered.
Tackling plastic pollution is essential for public health and urban resilience, especially in our major cities where the liveability deteriorates with every passing day. Practical, enforceable steps will determine whether the policy cleans up Bangladesh and helps us reduce the plastic burden.

item.title: Bangladesh needs more equity in healthcare. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A study by the Health Economics Unit (HEU) of the Ministry of Health has exposed something deeply disturbing in Bangladesh’s healthcare system: Wealthier citizens are increasingly claiming a larger share of benefits from public hospitals while poor families are being squeezed out.
Between 2016 and 2022, the share of public inpatient benefits going to the poorest two-fifths of households fell from 46% to 33%, whereas the wealthiest two-fifths saw their share rise from 28% to 38%.
When millions of ordinary Bangladeshis are already struggling under inflation, stagnant real wages, and economic strain, watching public healthcare fail those who need it most is simply unacceptable.
The financial fallout of this breakdown is devastating. Out-of-pocket medical expenses pushed over 1 crore Bangladeshis below the poverty line in 2022 - nearly double the 56 lakh impoverished by healthcare costs in 2005 - while over 90% of the poorest consumption group faced financial hardship from medical bills.
This is not what progress looks like for any nation, when low-income families are pushed into debt, asset sales, and prolonged illness.
Though the previous administration’s inability to address these issues or even identify how bad it was must be acknowledged, blaming past administrations alone cannot excuse ongoing inaction.
Metropolitan cities still lack accessible public primary and secondary facilities, pushing routine and emergency cases into crowded tertiary hospitals where connections and influence too often dictate access.
Government funding as a share of total health spending has also remained chronically low over the years. While the budget for health has increased this year, such an increase is meaningless if it does not reach those who need it most.
The Ministry of Health must work to restore genuine equity in public healthcare. Falling ill should never bankrupt the average citizen, and a more equitable nation is a better nation for all.

item.title: UN says violence against women rising, support services shrinking. [ dawn ]
item.description:
WASHINGTON: The United Nations on Wednesday launched its annual 16 Days of Activism campaign against gender-based violence, urging governments and societies to speak out against abuse, believe survivors and demand justice.

“Speak Out. Believe Survivors. De­­m­­and Justice,” read the message iss­ued by the UN to mark the first day of the global campaign, which runs until Dec 10, Human Rights Day. The campaign warned that too many survivors of violence and online harassment still face silence, disbelief and victim-blaming, allowing perpetrators to escape accountability.

“Every unanswered call for help, every dismissed report, and every unpunished act of violence” strengthens the web of impunity, the UN message said. It urged people to challenge attitudes that excuse violence, listen to survivors without judgment and respect their choices. Governments were asked to strengthen and enforce laws, fund support services and hold perpetrators and institutions accountable.

The campaign comes amid mounting concerns over violence against women in the digital and physical worlds, particularly in countries where social restrictions and inadequate protection systems discourage victims from seeking help.

A UN report on Pakistan, released on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on Nov 25, warned that online harassment was increasingly spilling into the physical world, contributing to femicide, suicide, physical violence and loss of employment.

The findings also showed how deeply entrenched social attitudes discourage women from challenging harassment. A survey in Pakistan found that 54pc of women believed women should leave their jobs if they faced harassment, while 83pc acknowledged that men often got away with harassing women.

The report said online abuse was not merely driving women and girls away from digital spaces but was also affecting their participation in professional and public life. It raised concerns about the response of companies, noting that most lacked clear policies to prevent and address online gender-based violence, while existing policies were often poorly implemented.

UN findings on attitudes in South Asia, including India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, pointed to a wider climate in which victims of harassment could face pressure to withdraw from public and professional life rather than expect perpetrators to be held accountable. The report also highlighted the global scale of violence. In the Arab states, 60pc of women internet users reported experiencing online violence.

Worldwide, an estimated 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2024 — an average of 137 every day, or one every 10 minutes — according to figures released by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime and UN Women.

The UN has urged women facing on­­­­line abuse to cut off contact with pe­­­r­­­p­­etrators and report online harassment, while calling on governments and technology companies to strengthen protections and accountability. The campaign’s launch also coincided with a renewed warning from UN Women about the deteriorating situation of women and girls in Afghanistan, where the risks of violence are increasing even as essential support services are disappearing because of funding cuts. In a statement marking the start of the campaign, UN Women Afghanistan urged governments and donors to increase support for Afghan women’s organisations, describing them as an essential lifeline for women and girls facing mounting social, economic and humanitarian pressures.

“Just as the risks of violence agai­nst women and girls are growing, the services they depend on are disappearing because of aid cuts,” said Su­­s­­an Ferguson, UN Women’s Special Representative in Afghanistan.

The UN said women’s organisations were particularly important in reaching survivors and providing services in circumstances where restrictions and economic hardship had sharply reduced their options.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

item.title: Bangladesh ties of 'great importance' to Pakistan, President and PM tell visiting parliament speaker. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh Parliament Speaker Hafizuddin Ahmad on Wednesday met with President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad, where the Pakistani leaders reaffirmed that Islamabad attached “great importance” to its ties with Dhaka.

The parliament speaker, accompanied by a parliamentary delegation, arrived in the country on Monday on a six-day official visit at the special invitation of National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq. This is the first official visit to Pakistan by a speaker of the Bangladesh parliament, according to the PM Office (PMO).

On Wednesday, Ahmad and his delegation called on President Zardari at Aiwan-i-Sadr, where the president noted that “Pakistan attaches great importance to its relations with Bangladesh, which are rooted in shared history, common faith and deep cultural and familial affinities”, his office said.

The Bangladeshi delegation included MP Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, chairman of the standing committee on foreign affairs; MPs Humam Quader Chowdhury, Muhammad Nazibur Rahman, Nilufar Chowdhury Moni, and Nasser Rahman; as well as Bangladesh High Commissioner to Pakistan Iqbal Hussain Khan.

On Pakistan’s side, the meeting was attended by Sadiq, Senators Sherry Rehman and Saleem Mandviwalla, MNAs Naveed Qamar and Dr Shazia Sobia Aslam Soomro, along with the convener of the Pakistan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship Group in NA.

Later, PM Shehbaz hosted a dinner at the PM House in honour of the visiting speaker and members of the parliamentary delegation.

“Welcoming the speaker and his delegation, the prime minister said that Pakistan attaches great importance to its fraternal ties with Bangladesh,” PMO said.

Recalling the shared history and cultural affinities between the two countries, the premier underscored the importance of closer institutional cooperation and stronger people-to-people contacts.

The prime minister noted that the “extensive engagements of the visiting parliamentary delegation in Pakistan indicate a huge scope of collaboration in parliamentary domain”, PMO said.

He emphasised that regular parliamentary exchanges would provide a robust foundation for closer bilateral cooperation across various avenues of mutual interest.

PMO also shared pictures of PM Shehbaz individually meeting the members of the visiting delegation.

‘Pakistan ready to extend defence cooperation with Bangladesh’

During his meeting with the visiting delegation, President Zardari emphasised the need to strengthen Pakistan-Bangladesh relations through expanded parliamentary exchanges, trade and economic cooperation, educational links and people-to-people contacts, calling for a “forward-looking approach based on sovereign equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit”.

He noted the “renewed momentum in bilateral relations, particularly in high-level exchanges, education, trade, culture and people-to-people contacts”, the Presidency said.

The president expressed hope for the early finalisation of around 26 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) “under consideration, which would provide an institutional framework for expanding bilateral cooperation”.

He “reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to extend defence cooperation with Bangladesh”, also highlighting the “considerable potential” for cooperation in agriculture, industry, food security, disaster management, digital governance and space research.

On connectivity, President Zardari welcomed the commencement in January of direct flights by Biman Bangladesh Airlines and emphasised the need to increase flight frequency and destinations in view of growing demand. He also called for exploring direct maritime links to facilitate trade and economic cooperation.

Discussing trade and economic relations, the president noted that bilateral trade remained below its potential.

Therefore, he called for effectively utilising existing mechanisms, including the Joint Economic Commission (JEC) and the Joint Working Group on Trade, to explore preferential trade arrangements and advance the priority areas identified during the JEC session held in October last year.

President Zardari noted that ongoing exports of Pakistani rice under the government-to-government agreement could serve as a basis for broader cooperation on food security and the supply of essential commodities.

“Pakistan, in line with Bangladesh’s request, is also ready to provide technical expertise for the refurbishment of sugar plants in Bangladesh,” the Presidency statement read.

President Zardari encouraged greater private-sector engagement across a range of sectors, including textiles, pharmaceuticals, leather, automobiles, construction materials, minerals, chemicals, ceramics and jute.

He offered Pakistan’s assistance in facilitating training for Bangladeshi parliamentary officials at the Pakistan Institute for Parliamentary Services (PIPS) and sharing its institutional expertise in operating a bicameral legislature.

The president expressed Islamabad’s desire to further strengthen parliamentary cooperation with Dhaka, as well as highlighted bilateral cooperation in the education and media sectors.

President Zardari welcomed progress under the China-Bangladesh-Pakistan Trilateral Mechanism, particularly the identification of 12 priority areas of cooperation during the Kunming meeting on June 19, 2025, the statement said.

He appreciated Bangladesh’s humanitarian gesture of hosting over one million Rohingya refugees, reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for their safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar in accordance with international law, and called upon the international community to ensure sustained humanitarian assistance.

The president expressed confidence that Ahmad’s visit would help advance bilateral relations and pave the way for more high-level exchanges between the two countries.

Meanwhile, Ahmad thanked the president for the warm welcome and hospitality extended to him and his delegation, according to the President House.

The speaker conveyed the greetings of Bangladesh President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

The statement said: “Recalling his personal memories of Pakistan, he underscored the importance of parliamentary diplomacy and expressed his desire to promote closer engagement between the two Parliaments through exchanges and regular institutional interaction.

“He also noted the popularity of Pakistani television dramas in Bangladesh, reflecting the cultural affinity between the peoples of the two countries.”

Relations between Islamabad and Dhaka have improved since the ouster of former Bangladeshi premier Sheikh Hasina, during whose tenure ties between the two countries remained shaky.

In February, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal attended the oath-taking ceremony of PM Rahman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).

Sadiq travelled to Dhaka in December 2025 for the funeral of the country’s first female prime minister Khaleda Zia. In August that year, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar had also visited Dhaka and met Yunus.
